12. Design Harmful Content Detection / Content Moderation (Facebook/Instagram Integrity)

Prompt as usually given: "Users post text, images and videos on a social platform. Design a system that detects harmful posts (violence, nudity, hate speech, self-harm, spam, misinformation) and removes or demotes them." Variants: comment toxicity, hateful memes (image + text), message moderation in DMs or dating apps, LLM guardrails, spam/abusive accounts (actor-level integrity).

Sourcing note: at review time (Oct 2026) web search was exhausted and ai.meta.com, about.fb.com, arxiv.org and bytebytego.com did not resolve from the build sandbox; only GitHub was reachable. Tags: (fetched) = read for this chapter; (repo-link) = URL appears verbatim in a fetched index (ByteByteGo's ml-bytebytego ch. 5 reference list [2] or the Engineer1999 list [11]); (ch-ref) = verified in another chapter; (known) = canonical paper by arXiv ID. Only "built it" company tags with a source are kept.

Company tags

Company Evidence Notes Source
Meta (Facebook, Instagram) Built it: WPIE, XLM-R + Linformer hate-speech models, Few-Shot Learner, TIES The canonical "house problem" for Meta MLE / integrity loops; ByteByteGo ch. 5 frames it on a Facebook-like platform [1][3][12][13][14][15][16][18]
Pinterest Built it: ML for misinformation, hate speech and self-harm; comment-health models Pin-level multimodal classifiers using PinSage/visual/text embeddings [20][21]
LinkedIn Built it: viral spam detection; isolation forest for abuse Spam / abusive actor framing [22][23]
Bumble, Nextdoor, Whatnot, Slack Built it: rude-message detection (multilingual DMs); harmful-comment prediction; GenAI marketplace-spam T&S; invite-spam blocking Variant systems for DM / comment / marketplace prompts (as indexed in [11]) [24][25][26][27]

Portals that cover it

Portal Treatment Link
ByteByteGo (Aminian & Xu, MLSDI), ch. 5 "Harmful Content Detection" Fullest treatment: multimodal early fusion, multi-task heads, BCE per task, prevalence / proactive rate, demotion vs violation services [1][2]
alirezadir Machine-Learning-Interviews, "mlsd-harmful-content" Condensed notes of the book chapter: 500M posts/day (~10K annotated), DistilmBERT + CLIP + VideoMoCo, gradient blending, focal loss; listed under "Harmful content / Spam detection" in the MLSD index [3][4]
Educative "Grokking the ML Interview" / Khang Pham MLSD Generic classification + ranking templates (no dedicated chapter verified); reuse the classifier pattern [5][6]
Exponent, Hello Interview, IGotAnOffer, Patrick Halina MLSD delivery frameworks and Meta MLE loop guides; no dedicated harmful-content chapter verified [7][8][9][10]
Engineer1999 curated case studies Index of real T&S / spam / fraud systems from 20+ company blogs [11]

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Source
Functional Input: a post (text, image(s), video, links, author). Output: per-category harm probabilities, action (remove / demote / send to review / allow), and a user-visible reason [1][3]
Harm categories Violence, nudity, hate speech (+ self-harm, spam, misinformation, bullying in variants) [1][3][20]
Out of scope (book) Harmful actors (fake / inauthentic accounts) and harmful acts; added as follow-ups [3][37]
Explainability Must tell the user which policy was violated; appeals flow [1][3]
Volume ~500M new posts/day (~6K posts/s avg, ~15-20K/s peak) [3] (book)
Labels ~10K posts hand-annotated (eval set); user reports ("natural labels") for the training set [3] (book)
Languages 100+ languages; multilingual encoder required [14][15]
Latency Varies by category: blocking classes (CSAM, terror) pre-publish p99 < ~200-500 ms; most classes near-real-time (seconds to minutes) after publish; re-scoring on virality [3] + typical assumption
Precision / recall Auto-remove needs very high precision (~95%+); demotion and review queues trade precision for recall typical assumption
Adversarial Evasion (text in image, leetspeak, re-encoded media), fast drift of new harm types [16][17]
Known-bad media Re-uploads of known CSAM / terror / NCII media matched by perceptual hash before any model [36]

Data & labels

Source Label type Pros Cons
Human reviewers (contractors) Gold, per-policy multi-label Accurate, policy-aware; book uses them for the eval set [3] Slow, costly (~10K labelled), reviewer wellbeing, disagreement; review tooling at scale [38]
User reports Natural, noisy positive Huge volume, fast Brigading, bias, many false reports; few negatives
Appeals overturned Label correction Fixes false positives Sparse, delayed
Hash banks (known violating media) Exact / near-dup positive (PDQ, TMK+PDQF, vPDQ; shared via ThreatExchange / HMA) [36] Zero-shot removal of re-uploads; cross-company sharing Only known content
Synthetic / LLM-generated Augmented positives New harm types, rare languages Distribution shift
Split strategy Time-based split; dedup by media hash across splits Avoids leakage of near-dup memes -

Features

Group Examples Encoding
Text Caption, hashtags, OCR from images, ASR from video, comments Multilingual transformer (DistilmBERT / XLM-R) [15][34][39]; comments aggregated
Image Pixels, detected objects, faces CLIP / SimCLR embedding [31][32]
Video Frames, audio VideoMoCo / frame-pooled image encoder + audio model [33]
Author Account age, followers, prior violations, report rate, profanity rate Numeric, bucketized; embedding of author
Interactions Likes, shares, comments, reports, view velocity Counts, ratios, time-decayed
Context Time of day, device, country/language, group/page type One-hot / embedding
Graph / actor Interaction sequences, cluster membership TIES-style temporal embeddings [18]

Model choices (baseline -> advanced)

Option Description Pros Cons
Rules + keyword lists Regex, blocklists, hash match Instant, explainable Low recall, easy to evade
Late fusion One model per modality, combine scores Simple, modular, debuggable Misses harm that only appears in combination (hateful memes [35][40])
Early fusion (book choice) Concatenate/attend modality embeddings, one classifier Captures cross-modal harm Harder to train, needs more data
Single binary classifier "harmful vs not" Simple No category -> no explanation; hard to set per-class thresholds
One model per category Separate binary models Independent tuning N models to train/serve/maintain
Multi-label single head One output layer, K sigmoids One model Shared features may not fit all classes
Multi-task (book choice) Shared trunk + per-task heads One model, data sharing helps rare classes, explainable Task interference; loss weighting
Foundation / few-shot (FSL) Policy-text entailment, LLM classifier [16][17] Fast adaptation to new policies Expensive; needs distillation for serving
Efficient transformer XLM-R with Linformer linear attention [14][28] Serve large multilingual model on every post Approximation; engineering cost
LLM-as-reviewer LLM judges borderline items with policy prompt Explainable, flexible Cost, latency, jailbreak / prompt-injection

Loss

Loss When
Sum of per-task BCE Default multi-task multi-label
Weighted BCE / class weights Severe imbalance (prevalence often < 0.1%)
Focal loss [30] Focus on hard, rare positives
Gradient blending [29] One modality dominating or overfitting in multimodal training
Label smoothing / noise-robust loss Noisy user-report labels

Offline metrics

Metric Why
PR-AUC per category Highly imbalanced data; ROC-AUC over-optimistic
Recall @ fixed precision (e.g. P >= 95%) Matches auto-remove threshold
F1 Single threshold summary
ROC-AUC Ranking quality, threshold-free
Per-language / per-market slices Fairness and coverage across 100+ languages
Calibration (ECE) Thresholds and severity x reach depend on calibrated probabilities

Online metrics / A-B

Metric Definition
Prevalence Harmful posts (or views) not prevented / all posts (views) [3][13]
Harmful impressions Views of harmful content before action
Proactive rate Detected by system / (system + user reports) [3][14]
Valid appeals rate Successful (reversed) appeals / removals (false positive proxy) [3]
User reports per 1K views Leading indicator of misses
Reviewer throughput / queue latency Ops health
Guardrails Engagement / creator retention of non-violating content (over-enforcement)
A-B caveat Holdouts limited by ethics; rely on shadow scoring + enforcement on small % + interleaved reviewer audits

Serving & latency budget

Stage Budget (typical) Notes
Hash match < 10 ms Perceptual hash lookup
Rules / cheap filters < 5 ms In-process
Feature fetch 10-20 ms Online KV store
Text encoder 10-30 ms Distilled / quantized, GPU or CPU
Image encoder 20-50 ms GPU batch, cached by media hash
Video seconds (async) Sample frames; score after publish
Fusion + heads < 5 ms Small MLP
Policy engine < 5 ms Thresholds per market
Total pre-publish (blocking classes) ~100-200 ms p99 Else async post-publish within seconds

Monitoring

Signal Action
Score distribution drift per category / language Alert, re-calibrate thresholds
Spike in user reports or appeals Trigger re-scoring, retraining
Reviewer disagreement with model Error analysis, label audit
New adversarial patterns (text-in-image, leetspeak) Add to red-team set, retrain
Latency / GPU saturation Fall back to cheaper text-only model
Prevalence dashboard (sampled reviewer audit) North-star tracking

Failure modes

Failure Mitigation
Adversarial evasion OCR/ASR, augmentation, hash near-dup, fast few-shot updates
Label noise and reviewer bias Multi-rater consensus, gold sets, noise-robust losses
Over-enforcement on dialects / minority languages Per-slice metrics, fairness thresholds
One modality dominates Gradient blending, modality dropout
New harm type (e.g. new scam, crisis event) FSL / LLM classifier, rules as stop-gap
Viral harmful post before review Prioritise by severity x predicted reach; re-score on velocity
Cold-start languages Cross-lingual transfer (XLM-R)
Feedback loop bias (only reported posts labelled) Random sampling for audits, active learning

Often-missed components (portal / real-system gaps)

Component What to add Source
Hash-sharing / hasher-matcher-actioner Maintain banks of PDQ / TMK+PDQF / vPDQ hashes, sync with industry exchanges, act on matches before the classifier [36]
Borderline-content demotion Content close to (but not violating) policy gets reduced distribution, not removal; separate threshold band [19]
Human review system at scale Queue routing by policy + language, reviewer tooling, wellbeing (blur, time limits), QA on reviewer accuracy [38]
Inauthentic-behaviour / actor layer Account-level classifiers (fake accounts, coordinated behaviour) feed author-risk into post scoring [18][37]
Benchmarks for multimodal hate Hateful Memes dataset and MMF baselines to test early vs late fusion [35][40]

Interviewer follow-ups

  • How do you handle severe class imbalance (prevalence well under 1%)?
  • Early vs late fusion: when does late fusion fail? (hateful memes)
  • Why multi-task over one model per category? How do you weight task losses?
  • How do you pick thresholds for remove vs demote vs human review?
  • How do you prioritise the human-review queue (severity x reach)?
  • How do you measure prevalence without labelling everything?
  • How do you handle 100+ languages and low-resource languages?
  • A new harm type appears today: how fast can you ship a classifier? (few-shot, rules, LLM)
  • How do you defend against adversarial users (text in images, re-encoded video)?
  • How do you deal with noisy, biased user-report labels and reviewer bias?
  • Pre-publish blocking vs post-publish detection: what goes where and why?
  • How would you detect harmful actors (fake accounts) rather than content? (TIES, graph)
  • How do you explain decisions to users and handle appeals?
  • How do you serve video cheaply at 500M posts/day?
  • How would you use an LLM in this system without blowing latency and cost budgets?
  • How would you share hashes of known violating media with other platforms, and how do you keep false matches low? [36]
  • How do you treat borderline content differently from violating content? [19]
  • How do you scale and quality-check the human review operation? [38]

Portal comparison

Portal Framing Model Metrics emphasis Distinctive points
ByteByteGo ch. 5 [1][2] Multimodal post classifier on social media Early fusion + multi-task heads, BCE sum PR-AUC offline; prevalence, proactive rate, appeals online Demotion vs violation services; gradient blending; focal loss
alirezadir notes [3] Same as book, condensed DistilmBERT + CLIP/SimCLR + VideoMoCo F1, PR-AUC, ROC-AUC Lists follow-ups: labeling bias, temporal signals, fake accounts, linear transformers
Meta engineering (real system) [13]-[17] Layered integrity stack WPIE, XLM-R + Linformer, FSL, TIES Prevalence, proactive detection rate Few-shot policy adaptation; RL-tuned enforcement
Pinterest engineering [20][21] Pin / comment health Embedding-based multi-head classifiers Precision at action thresholds Uses existing Pin embeddings; batch + online scoring
Generic MLSD guides (Exponent, Hello Interview, IGotAnOffer, Halina) [7]-[10] Framework-level Classifier template Precision/recall tradeoff Emphasis on clarifying requirements and delivery structure

13. Design Event Recommendation (Eventbrite / Meetup) with Location and Time Constraints

How the prompt is usually worded: "Design an event recommendation system like Eventbrite. Users should see personalized events they are likely to register for" (ByteByteGo ch. 7 [1][2]). The AIMLInterviews question bank lists it as "Event recommendation system (Eventbrite)" [3][4]. Variants: Meetup group and event suggestions, Facebook Events "Discover", local concerts and ticketing (Ticketmaster-style), "things to do this weekend near me".

Sourcing note: re-checked on 2026-10-14. Only GitHub hosts resolved; bytebytego.com, uber.com, kaggle.com, arxiv.org, huyenchip.com, hellointerview.com and developers.google.com did not. (fetched) = read through GitHub on that date. (ch-ref) = verified in an earlier chapter. (known) = canonical page not re-read here. No Eventbrite or Meetup engineering post could be verified, so no production system is claimed.

Company tags

Company What is reported Source
Eventbrite AIMLInterviews names the question "Event recommendation system (Eventbrite)" and gives a worked solution [3][4]
Eventbrite-style platforms ByteByteGo / Aminian & Xu MLSDI ch. 7, "Event Recommendation System", is framed on Eventbrite [1][2][5]
General MLE loops (Meta, Amazon) Portals list "design a recommender for X" as a standard MLSD round; events is one common instance [12][13]

Portals that cover it

Portal Treatment Link
ByteByteGo (Aminian & Xu, MLSDI ch. 7) Full chapter: pointwise LTR, location/time/social features, LR -> GBDT -> NN, mAP, online learning [1][2]

Chip Huyen, Khang Pham No event exercise. Closest: Airbnb location search (Huyen ex. 9); Airbnb Search Ranking and Estimate Delivery Time cases (Pham) [6][7]

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Source
Business goal Increase ticket sales / registrations [4]
Functional Personalized list of upcoming events for a user, near the user (or a chosen city), in a usable time window; free and paid events [1][4]
Users About 100M DAU, worldwide, many languages [4]
Catalog About 1M new events per month. Live inventory of a few million events at any time [4] / assumption
Latency About 200 ms end to end (proposed) [4]
QPS About 2-5k average, 20-50k peak (100M DAU x a few feed loads per day) assumption
Candidates Millions of events -> hundreds after location/time filtering -> top K (10-50) [4]
Key constraints Events are short-lived and expire, so every event is cold start. Strict geo and time windows. Capacity limits (sold out). Interaction data is sparse [1][4]
Freshness Registration counts and "friends attending" are streaming features. Model retrains daily or continually [1][5]
Privacy Location and friend graph are sensitive; obey consent and coarsen location [1]

Diagram 1: End-to-end architecture (online serving path)

Data & labels

Item Choice Notes / source
Training row (user, event, request time, features, label) One row per shown pair [4]
Positive Registered or bought a ticket after the impression, before the event starts [1][4]
Negative Shown, not registered (impressed negatives); optionally random in-radius events [1] / assumption
Weak labels Click, bookmark/like, share: auxiliary heads or weighted positives [1][4]
Imbalance Registrations are rare -> downsample negatives, focal or class-balanced loss [1][4][5]
Leakage Point-in-time features only; "registration count" must be the value at impression time [2] ref 26
Split Time-based (train on past weeks, validate on next week) assumption
Public data Kaggle "Event Recommendation Engine Challenge" (users, events, attendees, friends) [21]

Features

Group Examples Computation
Location Distance user-event, same city/state/country, walk score, transit score, gap from user's typical distance Online at request (distance) + batch (scores) [1][5]
Time Time remaining until start, gap from the user's typical lead time, travel time, day of week, hour Online [1][5]
Social Number/ratio of friends attending, friend invitations, host is a friend, similarity to friend-hosted events Streaming [1][4]
User Age (bucketized), gender, language, past registrations with time decay, user embedding Batch [4][5]
Event Category, price, duration, description text embedding, host popularity, registration count Batch + streaming [4]
Price Price, gap from the user's average paid price, free flag Batch [1][5]
User-event similarity Similarity of price, description and registration count to the user's past registered events; time-gap similarity Batch + online [4]
Geo encoding Lat/lng bucketing, geohash or cluster ids, distance to user's frequent places Batch [2] ref 9
Feature crosses Distance x time-to-start, price x user avg price (for LR / wide part) Batch [2] ref 22
Context Device, current location vs home location, weather (optional) Online / assumption

Model choices (baseline -> advanced)

Stage Model Pros Cons
0 Rule-based: nearest + soonest + most popular No training, works on day one Not personalized
1 Logistic regression Fast, interpretable Misses non-linear interactions (distance x time) [1][5]
2 GBDT (XGBoost / LightGBM) Strong on tabular features, little preprocessing [22] Hard to train continually on streaming data [1][4]
3 DNN pointwise ranker Non-linear, uses embeddings and text, fine-tunes incrementally Needs more data and tuning [1][5]
4 Two-tower retrieval + multi-task DNN ranker Personalized candidates beyond the geo filter; click + register heads More infrastructure; sampling bias in retrieval [17][18]
Alt Pairwise / listwise LTR (RankNet, LambdaMART) Optimizes ordering directly Harder to calibrate; ByteByteGo picks pointwise [1][8]

Loss functions

Loss When
Binary cross-entropy Default pointwise P(register) [1][5]
Focal loss Heavy imbalance; down-weights easy negatives [19]
Class-balanced loss Re-weights by effective number of samples per class [20]
Pairwise (RankNet) / LambdaRank Pairwise LTR alternative [2] refs 2-4 [8]
Multi-task sum: aBCE(click) + bBCE(register) Two-head ranker in Figure 13.3

Offline metrics

Metric Use Caveat
mAP Primary choice: binary relevance (registered or not) [1][4] Needs the full ranked list
nDCG@K Graded relevance (register > bookmark > click) Gain values must be chosen
Recall@K / Precision@K Candidate generation quality Ignore order [4]
MRR Only first relevant item Weak when many events fit [4]
Calibration / log loss Needed if scores feed thresholds or ads
Slices City, new events (< 24 h), new users, online vs in-person

Online metrics / A-B

Metric Type
Registration / ticket conversion rate per session Primary [1][4]
CTR Engagement [1][4]
Bookmark / like rate Engagement [1][4]
Revenue lift (paid tickets) Business [1][4]
Attendance (check-in) rate, refunds, no-shows Quality guardrail (assumption)
Host-side: share of events with at least 1 registration Marketplace fairness (assumption; see [16])
Latency p99, empty-result rate System guardrail

Serving & latency budget (assumption, p99, ~200 ms total [4])

Step Budget
Gateway + auth + context (geo lookup) 15 ms
Candidate generation (geo-time KV + ANN + social) 30 ms
Filtering (sold out, past, blocked) 10 ms
Feature fetch (feature store, batched) 40 ms
Ranking (~500 candidates, batched GBDT/DNN) 50 ms
Re-rank / policy + response 20 ms
Headroom 35 ms

Monitoring

What Signal
Data Feature null rate, geo lookup failures, stream lag for registration counts
Model Score distribution drift, calibration by city, mAP on daily holdout
Product CTR, conversion, empty results in low-density areas
Freshness Share of shown events that are sold out or already started (should be ~0)
Fairness Exposure share for small hosts and new events

Failure modes

Failure Mitigation
Cold start for every new event Content features (text embedding, category, host history), exploration slots [4]
New user with no history Popularity in their city + onboarding interests
Sparse areas (rural) Expand radius / time horizon, add online events
Showing sold-out or past events Streaming capacity feature + hard filter at serve time
Label leakage from registration counts Point-in-time feature joins [1]
Popularity feedback loop Exploration, freshness boost, host exposure caps [14]
Wrong user location (VPN, travel) Use device GPS when allowed; let user pick city
Privacy of location / friends Coarsen location, honour consent [2] ref 24

Interviewer follow-ups

  • Why is this a ranking problem and not plain classification? Pointwise vs pairwise vs listwise? [1][5]
  • Events expire within days or weeks. How do you handle constant cold start? [4]
  • Is location a hard filter or a feature? What happens in low-density areas?
  • How do you compute distance and travel time efficiently for hundreds of candidates? [4]
  • Which features are batch and which are streaming? How fresh must "registration count" be? [1][5]
  • How do you handle extreme class imbalance? Focal loss vs downsampling, and how do you recalibrate? [1][4]
  • GBDT or neural network, given continual learning needs? [1][4]
  • Why mAP rather than nDCG or MRR here? [1][4]
  • How do you avoid data leakage when building training data? [1]
  • How would you use the friendship graph and invitations? Any privacy risks? [1][4]
  • How do you add diversity (dates, categories) and freshness in re-ranking? [1][14]
  • This is a two-sided marketplace. How do you keep exposure fair to new or small hosts? [1][16]
  • How often do you retrain, and how would online learning work? [1][15]
  • How do you rank online/virtual events that have no location?
  • Paid promoted events: how do you blend them with organic ranking?
  • RSVP vs paid registration: are they the same label? What about age groups and many languages? [4]
  • Which features are batch vs real time, and what does each cost to serve? [2] ref 8
  • How do you train without exposing users' locations or friend lists (privacy-preserving ML)? [2] ref 24

alirezadir AIMLInterviews [3][4] Same, with explicit scale (100M DAU, 1M events/month, 200 ms) Rule-based filters, millions -> hundreds GBDT baseline, then NN mAP; CTR, conversion, revenue Lists open questions (RSVP vs register, age group, multilingual)

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Source
Functional Score each payment/authorization; return allow / review / 3DS step-up / block [1][2]
Functional Merchant-defined rules on top of score; explanations for decisions [1][2]
Functional Analyst review queue; feedback (disputes, manual labels) into training [4][9]
Latency Score in the authorization path, well under ~100 ms end to end [1]
Throughput 5k-50k payments/s peak (Black Friday 3-5x average) typical assumption
Feature count 1,000+ signals per payment at Stripe Radar [1]
Entities 100M-1B cards, devices, emails, IPs; millions of merchants typical assumption
Fraud base rate 0.05%-0.5% of transactions (extreme imbalance) typical assumption
Label delay Chargebacks arrive days to ~90+ days after the charge [1][3]
Availability 99.99%; fail-open or fail-to-rules if model is down typical assumption
Cost asymmetry Missed fraud = amount + fee; false decline = lost revenue + churn [3][6]

Data & labels

Source Label / use Caveat
Fraudulent chargebacks Positive label (strongest) Delay of weeks; friendly fraud noise
Early fraud warnings / issuer reports Faster positive signal Coverage varies by network
Manual review outcomes Positive/negative Biased to borderline scores
Refunds flagged as fraud by merchant Weak positive Merchant-dependent
Matured non-disputed charges Negative after window Blocked charges never get labels
Exploration holdout (tiny % allowed) Unbiased estimate of true fraud rate Costs real money
Weak supervision (heuristic labeling functions) Extra noisy labels for unlabeled/new patterns [27] Label noise; needs denoising

Features

Group Examples
Transaction amount, currency, MCC, card-present flag, time of day, amount vs merchant avg
Velocity (stream) txns per card/IP/device/email in 1m, 1h, 24h; distinct cards per device
Identity / device device fingerprint, browser, IP geo vs billing country, proxy/VPN flag
Card / issuer BIN country, card age on network, prior declines, prior disputes
Network / graph shared device/IP with known fraud, connected-component size, fraud-ring cluster [3][12]
Behavioral checkout dwell time, typing speed, copy-paste of card number
Merchant merchant dispute rate, vertical, account age

Model choices

Stage Model Pros Cons
Baseline Rules + logistic regression Explainable, fast Low recall, brittle
Standard GBDT (XGBoost/LightGBM) Strong on tabular, fast CPU inference Weak on raw sequences/ids
Hybrid Wide & Deep (GBDT + DNN) Combines memorization + generalization Two systems to maintain [1]
Advanced Single deep net (residual MLP + embeddings) Scales with features, one pipeline [1][11] Needs more data, explainability tooling
Sequence RNN/Transformer over event history; customer-journey embeddings [25] Captures behavior change, ATO Latency, state storage
Graph GNN / graph features, similarity clustering Catches rings, mule networks [3][6][12] Real-time graph cost
Unsupervised Isolation forest, autoencoder, graph anomaly Novel attacks, no labels [10][13] High FP, hard to tune

Loss

Option When
Weighted binary cross-entropy Default; weight positives or by dollar amount
Focal loss Extreme imbalance, many easy negatives
Cost-sensitive / amount-weighted loss Optimize dollars, not counts
Multi-task BCE (fraud, dispute, ATO) Shared tower, sparse fraud labels
Calibration (Platt/isotonic) after training Thresholds must map to stable probabilities

Offline metrics

Metric Why
PR-AUC (not ROC-AUC) Base rate under 1%
Recall at fixed FPR / block rate Matches business constraint (e.g. block 0.5%)
Dollar-weighted recall / $ fraud caught Large tickets matter more
Calibration (ECE, reliability) Thresholds and merchant rules depend on it
Per-slice metrics Country, MCC, new vs existing card, merchant size
Time-based backtest Train on t, test on t+k; detects decay

Online metrics & A-B

Metric Direction
Fraud chargeback rate (bps of volume) Down
False-positive / good-user decline rate Down [6]
Authorization / conversion rate Up
Manual review volume & precision Down / up
Net $ = fraud saved - lost good revenue - review cost Up
A-B design Randomize by merchant or card; long horizon because labels lag; use early-warning proxies

Serving & latency budget

Step Budget (typical assumption)
Enrichment (BIN, geo-IP, device) 5-10 ms
Online feature store reads (KV, parallel) 5-15 ms
Graph lookups (1-2 hop, cached) 5-15 ms
Model inference (GBDT CPU or small DNN) 5-20 ms
Policy / rules engine 1-5 ms
Total p99 under ~100 ms [1]
Fallback Timeout -> rules-only or last cached score; fail-open for low amounts

Monitoring

Signal Action
Score distribution / block-rate drift Alert; recalibrate thresholds
Feature null-rate, freshness lag of stream aggregates Page on-call; fall back to rules
Early-warning fraud rate by segment Detect new attack campaigns
Analyst-confirmed precision on review queue Track quality daily
Shadow vs prod disagreement Gate model promotion [4]
Per-merchant spikes Auto-tighten rules for that merchant
Attack-campaign detector (time-series anomaly on fraud signals) Propose rules; analyst approves before deploy (human in loop) [8]
Entity-level anomaly watch (riders/drivers/cards) Flag risky entities missed by txn model [9]

Failure modes

Failure Mitigation
Label delay -> stale model Proxy labels (early warnings, reviews); frequent retrains
Selection bias (blocked txns unlabeled) Exploration holdout, counterfactual/IPS weighting
Adversarial adaptation Fast retrain, rules for hotfixes, graph/ring features
Train/serve skew in velocity features Same feature definitions offline and online, point-in-time joins
Feedback loop from own decisions Log propensity; keep randomized holdout
Friendly fraud mislabeled as fraud Separate dispute reason codes; multi-task heads
Cold start (new merchant/card) Network-level priors, population features
Explainability / regulation Reason codes, SHAP, merchant-facing insights [1][15]

Interviewer follow-ups

  • Labels arrive 30-90 days late: how do you train and evaluate on recent data?
  • You never see the outcome of blocked transactions: how do you estimate true recall?
  • How do you choose the threshold, and does it differ per merchant or per amount?
  • ROC-AUC is 0.99 but the business is unhappy: why, and what metric do you use instead?
  • How do you compute "transactions per card in the last hour" consistently online and offline?
  • How do you detect a fraud ring of many new cards using one device or IP?
  • Fraudsters change tactics within days: how fast can you retrain and ship safely?
  • How do you combine merchant rules with the ML score without double counting?
  • What happens if the feature store or model server times out in the auth path?
  • How do you run an A-B test when the outcome takes two months?
  • How do you explain a decline to a merchant or regulator?
  • How do you handle a new merchant with no history (cold start)?
  • When do you add a 3DS step-up instead of a hard block?
  • Would you use a GNN online, or precompute graph features? Why?
  • How do you separate friendly fraud from true fraud in labels?
  • A card-testing attack sends thousands of tiny charges from one merchant: which features and rules catch it?
  • How do analysts and auto-generated rules coexist with the model, and who can ship a rule in minutes? [8]
  • How would you reuse one model across products/domains without hurting good-user approval? [6]

15. Design ETA / Delivery Time Prediction (Uber, DoorDash, Amazon Delivery)

Sourcing note: in this review run, company blogs, arXiv and ACM could not be fetched (proxy denial) and the web-search budget was spent. The GitHub portal repositories [7][8][9][12] were cloned and checked line by line. Company and paper references ([1]-[6], [10], [11], [13]) use their canonical URLs; four of them ([1], [10], [11], [13]) are also linked from those portal repositories. Rows marked "typical assumption" are standard interview estimates, not quoted numbers.

Company tags

Company Evidence Ref
Uber / Uber Eats DeepETA: a transformer that predicts a residual on top of the routing-engine ETA [1][2]
Uber Eats Trip inferences and ML (food prep time) used to optimize delivery times [11]
DoorDash Multi-task deep ETA models with probabilistic outputs; long-tail ETA work [3][13]
Google Maps GNN over road "supersegments" for travel-time ETA [4][5]
DiDi Wide-Deep-Recurrent (WDR) travel-time model [6]
Generic question "Food delivery time approximation" is a sample MLSD question [7][12]
Generic question "Estimate Delivery time" is a module of Khang Pham's ML design course [8]

Amazon, Instacart, Lyft and Grab use the same pattern in interviews, but this run found no source that ties them to the question, so they are not tagged.

Portals that cover the problem:

Portal Coverage Ref
khangich/machine-learning-interview "Estimate Delivery time" course module (paid, rebrand.ly/mldesign); README lists Uber Eats and DoorDash dispatch reading [8]
alirezadir (AIMLInterviews / Machine-Learning-Interviews) "Food delivery time approximation" listed under "Other" sample questions; links Uber DeepETA [7][12]
chiphuyen/machine-learning-systems-design Generic framework only (setup, data, modeling, serving); no ETA case [9]

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Source
Functional Predict ETA before the order or request (quote) and refresh it during the trip [1][3]
Functional Serve several ETA stages (browse page, checkout, post-checkout tracking) [3]
Functional Decompose: prep time + courier to store + wait + store to customer [10][11]
Functional Output a point estimate plus an interval ("25-35 min") [3]
Consumers Users (quote), dispatch/matching, pricing, supply positioning [1][10]
Latency Low single-digit ms per model call; ETA is called many times per request [1]
Throughput Uber: DeepETA is described as one of the highest-QPS models at the company [1]
Throughput 50k-500k ETA calls/s at peak (dispatch scores many driver-order pairs) typical assumption
Scale Millions of orders a day, millions of road segments, 100k+ stores typical assumption
Accuracy Minimize MAE; bound the late rate (under-prediction costs more) [1][3]
Freshness Traffic and store-load features updated within seconds to minutes [3][4]

DIAGRAM 1: Online ETA serving path

Data & labels

Item Detail Ref
Label (rides) Actual pickup or trip duration from trip events [1]
Label (delivery) created -> dropoff; per-leg: prep, courier to store, wait, drive [10][11]
Prep-time label Not observed directly; inferred from courier arrival and pickup events [11]
Residual label actual - routing-engine ETA (narrower, easier target) [1][2]
Label delay Known only after completion (30-60 min); join by order id typical assumption
Noise Cancelled orders, GPS drift, courier batching, manual "picked up" taps typical assumption
Splits Time-based; hold out whole days; check per city and holidays typical assumption
Volume Hundreds of millions of historical trips for training [1]

Features

Group Examples Freshness
Route Distance, base routing ETA, turn count, highway share per request
Traffic Live segment speeds, historical speeds by hour of week seconds-minutes [4]
Geo Origin/destination geohash at several resolutions, hashed embeddings static [1]
Time Hour, weekday, holiday, minute of day (cyclical) per request
Store Historical prep time, open orders, cuisine, order size minutes [3][11]
Supply Idle couriers nearby, courier distance, acceptance rates seconds [10]
Real-time load Orders in the last N minutes at the store and in the area (long-tail signal) minutes [13]
Context Weather, events, product type (Eats vs rides, scheduled vs ASAP) minutes

Model choices

Stage Model Pros Cons
Baseline 0 Routing engine ETA (graph shortest path) No training, explainable Misses prep time and traffic quirks
Baseline 1 Historical average by (store, hour) + routing Trivial No interactions, cold start
Classic GBDT (XGBoost/LightGBM) on tabular features Strong, fast, interpretable Hits a ceiling at Uber's data scale; Uber moved from XGBoost to DeepETA [1]
Deep residual Transformer/MLP predicting the residual over base ETA Scales with data, embeddings for geo Needs careful latency work [1]
Graph GNN over road supersegments Captures how traffic spreads in space Heavy infra; mainly for the travel leg [4][5]
Sequence Wide-Deep-Recurrent over route links Uses the link sequence Long sequences, slower [6]
Multi-task / probabilistic Shared encoder, stage or leg heads, distribution output One model for many ETA stages; intervals for quotes Harder to train and calibrate [3]

Loss

Loss Why
MAE / L1 Robust to outliers, matches the MAE KPI
Huber Smooth near 0, robust tails
Asymmetric Huber Penalize lateness more than earliness; tunable [1]
Quantile (pinball) for p50/p80/p90 Gives intervals and SLA-aligned quotes
Distribution NLL (predict distribution parameters) Full probabilistic forecast for quotes [3]
Multi-task sum + leg consistency Total and sum of legs agree

Offline metrics

Metric Notes
MAE, RMSE, MAPE Overall and sliced by city, hour, distance, product
p50 / p90 absolute error The tail matters for user trust
Late rate Share of orders where actual > quoted (or > upper bound)
Interval coverage & width Calibration of p10-p90 bands
Long-tail error Error on the slowest few percent of orders (rush, storms) [13]
Bias by segment Systematic early or late in new cities, rain, peak

Online metrics & A-B

Metric Direction
On-time rate vs quote Up
Conversion (checkout after quote) Up; pessimistic ETAs lower it
Cancellations, "where is my order" support contacts Down
Courier wait time at store (dispatch quality) Down [10]
Guardrails: p99 latency, error rate, revenue No regression
Design Switchback or geo-cluster experiments (dispatch network effects)

Serving & latency budget

Step Budget (typical assumption)
Routing engine base ETA 5-20 ms
Online feature fetch (Redis/Cassandra) 2-5 ms
Model inference (CPU, linear attention) 1-5 ms [1]
Post-processing, calibration, rules <1 ms
Total per quote under ~50 ms; dispatch scores thousands of pairs in batches
Tactics Residual on base ETA, embedding caches, quantized or distilled models, fall back to routing ETA on timeout

Monitoring

Signal Action
Rolling MAE and late rate by city-hour (once labels arrive) Alert, roll back
Feature drift (traffic feed outage, stale store load) Fall back to historical features
Prediction shift (mean ETA jump) Check map or routing releases
Interval coverage Recalibrate quantiles
Latency, timeouts, fallback rate Scale out or simplify the model

Failure modes

Failure Mitigation
Feedback loop: the quote shapes courier behavior and dispatch Log exploration, causal eval, per-leg labels
Label leakage (future features in training) Point-in-time feature snapshots
Cold-start stores or new cities Hierarchical fallbacks (cuisine, region), shared embeddings
Extreme events (storms, concerts, rush peaks) Real-time load features, surge flags, wider intervals [13]
Routing-engine changes shift the base ETA Retrain the residual model, monitor bias
Quotes that are consistently optimistic Asymmetric loss, quantile quoting, buffers
Batched multi-order trips Explicit batch features or a separate model

Interviewer follow-ups

  • Why predict a residual over the routing engine instead of the raw ETA? [1]
  • How do you split a delivery ETA into legs, and do you train one model or many?
  • How do you handle the higher cost of being late than early?
  • How would you output an interval instead of one number, and calibrate it? [3]
  • How do you encode lat/lng and very high-cardinality geo IDs? (geohash, feature hashing) [1]
  • How do you get real-time traffic and store-load features into the model fast?
  • How do you avoid leakage when building training data from logs?
  • How do you update the ETA mid-trip as new GPS pings arrive?
  • XGBoost vs a deep model: when does the deep model win, and at what latency? [1]
  • How do you A/B test ETA changes given dispatch network effects? (switchback)
  • How do you handle a new city or a new restaurant with no history?
  • How do you keep accuracy on long-tail events such as storms or rush peaks? [13]
  • How do you label food prep time when nobody records it? [11]
  • What happens if the traffic feed or feature store goes down? (fallbacks)
  • How does ETA feed dispatch, pricing and batching decisions? [10][11]
  • Which metric would you report to the business, and why not only MAE?

16. Design Email Spam / Abuse / Bot Detection (Gmail Spam Filter, Twitter/X Bots)

Prompt as usually given: "Design a system that classifies incoming email as spam / phishing / ham" or "Detect spam bots and fake accounts on a social network (Twitter/X, LinkedIn, Facebook)." Variants: comment / DM spam, invite spam (Slack), phone-lead spam (Zillow), viral spam posts (LinkedIn), fake-account registration, coordinated inauthentic behaviour.

Sourcing note: at review time only github.com was reachable from the build sandbox (arxiv.org, medium.com, company blogs failed DNS) and web search was exhausted. Each reference carries a tag. (fetched) = GitHub page re-read during review. (repo-link) = URL appears verbatim in a fetched GitHub index (ByteByteGo ml-bytebytego, Engineer1999 case-study list, Botometer README, RETVec README). (ch-ref) = URL verified in another chapter of this atlas. (known) = canonical page cited from memory, not re-fetched. "Asked by" tags without a cited interview report were removed. Numbers marked "typical assumption" are standard interview estimates.

Company tags

Company Evidence Notes Source
Google (Gmail) Built it: RETVec robust text vectorizer (~200K params) deployed for Gmail spam per Google's blog [1]; RETVec repo itself does not name Gmail [2] Canonical "email spam" system; [1] reports ~38% higher spam detection, ~19% fewer false positives and ~83% less TPU use vs prior vectorizer (not re-fetched) [1][2][3]
X / Twitter Built it: open-sourced trust-and-safety models (pNSFWMedia, pNSFWText, pToxicity, pAbuse) and visibility filters; no spam/bot model published README: "several more models and rules" withheld "because of the adversarial nature of this area" [4][5]
Meta (Facebook, Instagram) Built it: inauthentic-behaviour policy, integrity survey, TIES temporal interaction embeddings, abusive-account detection framework Actor-level (account) detection; ByteByteGo ch. 5 cites these as follow-ups [6][7][8][9][10]
LinkedIn Built it: fake-account detection, isolation forest for abuse, viral spam content detection Two-stage: at registration + post-registration activity [11][12][13]
Pinterest, Slack, Zillow Built it: spam clustering + automated rule creation; invite-spam ML; SpectroBrain phone-spam (semi-supervised) Good "variant" systems [14][15][16]
Academic (Indiana Univ. OSoMe) Botometer: public Twitter bot-score service (v1-v4, BotometerLite); Botometer X is archival, scores from data collected before June 2023 Canonical bot-detection features and paper trail [17][18][19]

Portals that cover it

Portal Treatment Link
alirezadir Machine-Learning-Interviews Lists "Harmful content / Spam detection system" and "Fraud detection system" under "Other"; harmful-content notes list "detect fake accounts" as other topic [20][21]
ByteByteGo (Aminian & Xu, MLSDI) ch. 5 Harmful content detection; harmful actors / fake accounts / abusive-account framework as follow-ups [22][23]
Educative "Grokking the ML Interview" / Khang Pham MLSD Classification template; "Fraud detection (TBD)" heading, empty, in Khang Pham's repo [24][25][26]
Chip Huyen MLSD exercises Closest: exercise 2, fraud detection from labelled credit-card transactions [27]
Exponent, Hello Interview, IGotAnOffer, Patrick Halina General MLSD frameworks; integrity/spam frequently used as example classification prompt [28][29][30][31]
Engineer1999 curated case studies Index of spam / abuse / fraud systems from company blogs [32]

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Source
Functional (email) For each inbound message: spam / phishing / malware / promo / ham; action = reject at SMTP, send to Spam folder, warn banner, deliver typical assumption
Functional (bots) For each account: bot / fake / compromised score; action = challenge (CAPTCHA, phone verify), rate-limit, shadow-limit, suspend [11][17] + typical assumption
Entities scored Message, sender (IP, domain), account, URL, cluster (campaign) typical assumption
Email volume Billions of messages/day; ~100K-300K msg/s peak (interview assumption) typical assumption
Account volume ~1M sign-ups/day; ~500M daily actions to score (posts, follows, DMs) typical assumption
Latency Email: p99 < 100-200 ms inside SMTP accept path; account sign-up: < 100 ms; batch account sweeps: hourly/daily typical assumption
Precision False positives (ham in spam, real user banned) are costly; target FPR < 0.1% on ham typical assumption
Adversarial Attackers adapt in hours: obfuscation (homoglyphs, LEET, typos), image spam, account farms [1][2][4]
Languages 100+ languages; vocabulary-free text encoder preferred [2][3]
Privacy Email content is private: limited human labeling, on-device or aggregate features, data retention limits typical assumption
Sender policy (Gmail, 2024) Bulk senders (>5K msgs/day to Gmail) must pass SPF + DKIM + DMARC, offer one-click unsubscribe, keep Postmaster spam rate < 0.3%: authentication results become hard features / gates [34]

                                             |
          +----------------+-----------------+-----------------+---------------+
          v                v                 v                 v               v
   +------------+   +------------+   +---------------+   +------------+  +------------+
   | p(spam)    |   | p(phish)   |   | p(malware)    |   | p(promo)   |  | campaign   |
   | sigmoid    |   | sigmoid    |   | sigmoid       |   | sigmoid    |  | embedding  |
   +------------+   +------------+   +---------------+   +------------+  | (for LSH)  |
                                                                         +------------+
   Loss = sum_k w_k * BCE_k (focal for rare phish/malware) + optional contrastive term

Data & labels

Source Type Pros Cons
"Report spam" / "Not spam" clicks Explicit, user Huge volume, fresh Noisy (users report newsletters), biased to visible mail
Implicit (delete unread, never opened, unsubscribe) Weak Free Very noisy; use as features or low-weight labels
Honeypot / spam-trap inboxes, seeded accounts Ground truth spam High precision, early Not representative of targeted spam
Analyst review (sampled, privacy-reviewed) Gold Accurate eval set Expensive, privacy constraints
Enforcement outcomes (suspended, appealed) Account labels Strong for bots Delayed, feedback-loop bias
Rule / blocklist hits Heuristic Cheap Model learns the rule; keep held-out
Semi-supervised / clustering Propagated Scales labels to campaigns Error propagation [16][14]

Features

Group Examples
Sender reputation IP / ASN / domain age, SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass, historical spam rate, volume spikes, bounce rate
Content Raw text via robust char encoder, subject length, ALL CAPS ratio, HTML/text ratio, hidden text, OCR from images
URL / attachment Domain age, redirect chain, URL shortener, known-bad hash, file type, macro presence; async sandbox detonation verdict for unknown attachments (feeds post-delivery re-scan)
Recipient context Sender in contacts, prior replies, user's own report history, # recipients
Campaign Near-duplicate cluster size (MinHash), burst rate, # distinct senders sharing template
Account behaviour (bots) Account age, followers/following ratio, posts per hour, inter-action time entropy, default profile, username randomness [17][18]
Graph (bots) Shared device/IP edges, clustering coefficient, reciprocity, neighbour bot scores [7][8]

Model choices (baseline -> advanced)

Stage Model Tradeoffs
0 Rules + blocklists + hash match Instant, explainable; brittle, easily evaded
1 Naive Bayes / logistic on bag-of-words Classic baseline; cheap; obfuscation breaks it
2 GBDT (XGBoost/LightGBM) on reputation + engineered features Strong on tabular signals; fast; weak on raw text
3 Deep text model (char-CNN / RETVec + transformer, multilingual) Robust to typos/homoglyphs; costlier; needs GPU/TPU budget [2][3]
4 Multimodal multi-task (text + URL + image + sender) Shares signal across spam/phish/malware; harder to debug
5 Graph / temporal models for actors (GNN, TIES) Catches coordinated bots; offline/near-line [8]
6 Unsupervised (isolation forest, clustering + auto-rules) Finds new attacks without labels [12][14]
7 LLM-as-judge for borderline / analyst assist Rich reasoning; too slow/expensive for every message
8 Few-shot adaptable large model (Meta Few-Shot Learner style) New abuse policy enforced from a handful of examples in weeks, not months; heavy, used near-line [35]

Loss

Choice When
Weighted BCE per head Default multi-label (spam, phish, malware, promo)
Focal loss Rare classes (phish, malware) with extreme imbalance [33]
Sample weights by label source Honeypot > analyst > user report > implicit
Cost-sensitive / asymmetric FP (ham to spam) costs more than FN
Contrastive / triplet on campaign pairs Learn campaign embeddings for clustering

Offline metrics

Metric Why
Recall at fixed FPR (e.g. FPR <= 0.1% on ham) Operating-point metric that matches the business
PR-AUC Imbalanced data; better than ROC-AUC
Per-slice FPR (language, sender type, new domains) Fairness to legit small senders
Adversarial robustness Accuracy on perturbed (typo/homoglyph) test set [2]
Calibration (ECE) Thresholds and policy engine depend on calibrated scores
Time-split holdout Detect decay against newest attacks

Online metrics / A-B

Metric Direction
Spam-in-inbox rate (user "report spam" per 1K inbox mails) Down
Ham-in-spam rate ("not spam" clicks per 1K spam-folder mails) Down (guardrail)
Phishing click-through on delivered mail Down
Bot prevalence (sampled audit) / fake sign-ups per day Down
Prevalence (violating views / all views) and proactive rate (caught by system / all actioned) Down / Up [21][22]
False suspensions, appeal overturn rate Down (guardrail)
Time-to-detect new campaign Down
Engagement of legit senders / legit new users Neutral (guardrail)
  • A/B caveat: adversaries see both arms; randomize by recipient, run short tests, and favour shadow mode + back-testing.

Serving & latency budget (email, p99 ~150 ms)

Step Budget
SMTP edge + reputation lookup 10 ms
Rules / hash / blocklist 5 ms
Parse MIME, URLs, OCR (async for heavy images) 25 ms
Feature store fetch 15 ms
Stage-1 GBDT 2-5 ms
Stage-2 deep model (only uncertain ~10-20%) 20-40 ms on accelerator
Policy engine + write decision 10 ms
Headroom ~40 ms
  • Post-delivery re-scan: messages already delivered can be moved to Spam when a campaign is later detected ("zero-hour" retro-actions).

Monitoring

Signal Action
Score distribution shift per sender segment Alert, re-calibrate thresholds
Sudden rise in "not spam" clicks Auto-rollback model / threshold
New cluster growth rate Analyst queue, auto-rule
Feature freshness (reputation lag) Page on-call
Label pipeline delay Pause retraining
Per-language precision from sampled audits Retrain / add data

Failure modes

Failure Mitigation
Adversarial obfuscation (homoglyphs, LEET, zero-width chars) Robust char encoder (RETVec), Unicode normalization, adversarial augmentation [2][3]
Image-only spam OCR + image embeddings
Account warm-up (bots act human first) Long-horizon behaviour models, graph signals
Feedback loop (only mail in inbox gets reported) Exploration sample, honeypots, analyst audits
Legit bulk senders (newsletters) flagged Promo class separate from spam; sender reputation; one-click unsubscribe
Label noise from user reports Label model, per-user reliability weights
Model leaks via probing Randomized thresholds, delayed actions, no fine-grained error messages
Compromised legit accounts Account-takeover detection (login anomalies), not only content
Cold start new domains/IPs Prior from ASN/registrar; conservative throttling

Interviewer follow-ups

  • How do you get labels when email content is private and cannot be freely reviewed?
  • How do you handle "report spam" noise (users reporting newsletters they subscribed to)?
  • Spammers adapt in hours: how do you detect a brand-new campaign with zero labels?
  • How would you make the text model robust to homoglyphs, typos and zero-width characters?
  • Rules vs ML: when do you keep a hand-written rule, and how do rules feed the model?
  • Choose the threshold: what is the cost of a false positive vs a false negative here?
  • Why not one model for spam, phishing and malware? Multi-task vs separate models.
  • How do you evaluate offline when attackers react to your deployed model?
  • Bots: what features separate a bot from a power user or a legit automated account?
  • How would you use the graph (shared IPs/devices, follow graph) to find bot rings?
  • How do you avoid feedback loops where only inboxed mail can be reported?
  • How do you serve billions of messages/day under 150 ms? What runs in the cascade?
  • How do you A/B test when the adversary observes both arms?
  • How would you add an LLM, and where in the cascade would it sit?
  • How do you handle appeals and false suspensions, and use them as labels?
  • How do sender-authentication rules (SPF/DKIM/DMARC, bulk-sender spam-rate caps) change what the model must learn? [34]
  • How do you measure prevalence when most spam is never seen by users? (sampled audits, proactive rate) [21][22]

17. Design Google Street View Face and License-Plate Blurring (Object Detection Pipeline)

A privacy pipeline that finds every face and license plate in billions of panoramic street images and blurs them before publication. Unlike most chapters, there is no user request in the loop. The "serving path" is a high-throughput batch inference pipeline, the model is an object detector, and the business metric favours recall (a missed face is a privacy incident; an extra blur costs little).

Research note: in the review pass only github.com URLs could be fetched (other hosts failed DNS resolution, and the search budget was used up). Tags: (verified) = fetched in the review; (ch-ref) = verified in an earlier chapter of this atlas; (known) = a stable arXiv or paper URL not re-fetched. Numbers in tables are typical assumptions unless they carry a citation.

Company tags

Company What is reported Source
Google Owns the real system: automatic face and plate blurring in Street View since 2008 (ICCV 2009 paper) [2] [3]
Google (interview) ByteByteGo ch. 3 is titled "Google Street View Blurring System" [1] [6]
Meta Real comparable system: EgoBlur, open-source face and plate blurring for Project Aria egocentric data [25]
Generic (any company) alirezadir lists "Image blurring system" as a sample CV design question, with no company named [4]

Portals that cover it

  • ByteByteGo, Aminian & Xu, Machine Learning System Design Interview, ch. 3, "Google Street View Blurring System". This is the canonical write-up [1]. Its 27-item reference list on GitHub covers R-CNN family, YOLO, SSD, DETR, NMS, COCO eval, distributed training, GDPR, face-detection bias, active learning, human-in-the-loop [6].
  • alirezadir / Machine-Learning-Interviews: CV section with two-stage (R-CNN, Fast/Faster R-CNN) and one-stage (YOLO, SSD) detectors, mAP, and "Image blurring system" as a sample question [4].
  • Educative "Grokking the ML Interview" covers the related self-driving image segmentation case [7].
  • Exponent, Hello Interview, Patrick Halina: generic delivery frameworks that this chapter maps onto a CV pipeline [8] [9] [10].
  • Not covered: Chip Huyen's MLSD exercises have image retrieval and image classification but no detection or blurring exercise [12]; khangich/machine-learning-interview has no CV design case [13].

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Source
Functional Input: street-level image or panorama. Output: the same image with every face and plate blurred [1]
Objects 2 classes (human face, license plate). Optional extras: house numbers, people in private settings [1] [2]
Primary objective High recall at a fixed precision floor. A missed face is a privacy breach [1] [2]
Reported quality (Google 2009) About 89% of faces and 94-96% of plates blurred automatically [2]
Latency Not user-facing: batch, hours to days before publication [1]
Throughput About 1M+ new images a day; every panorama is about 75-100 MP (stitched from 8-15 cameras) assumption
Total corpus Tens of billions of images, re-run whenever the model is upgraded assumption
Labelled data About 1M images with bounding-box annotations (ByteByteGo's stated assumption) [1]
Compliance GDPR / local privacy law: raw imagery retention limits, deletion on request [6]
User feedback "Report a problem" button: users ask for extra blurring (whole house, person, car) [3]
Fairness Recall must hold across skin tones, ages, poses, plate formats from 100+ countries assumption
Cost GPU-hours per image dominate; tile and batch to keep accelerator use above 70% assumption

  • No feature store: the "features" are pixels plus metadata (camera id, GPS, time).
  • The raw store is tightly access-controlled. Only blurred derivatives reach serving [2] [3].
  • If the model is upgraded, the corpus is backfilled. Blurs are additive (new boxes are unioned with old ones), so the new model never un-blurs anything.

 | (per anchor/point,  | | (per anchor/point,  |  | detectors (frontal +    |

            |                       |                          | many candidates

                                                  | cascade) + blur         |
                                                  +-------------------------+
                                                  89% faces, 94-96% plates

Data & labels

Source Label type Size / volume Notes Source
Human-annotated Street View images Bounding boxes, 2 classes About 1M images ByteByteGo assumption. Annotate tiles, keep "ignore" regions for crowds [1]
Public face sets (WIDER FACE) Boxes, with blur, pose and occlusion attributes 32k images, 394k faces Pretraining and hard tiny-face cases [18]
Public plate sets (country specific) Boxes / corners Varies Plate shapes and scripts differ by country assumption
User "Report a problem" Image-level request plus a region Ongoing Noisy, and covers more than faces and plates (houses, cars) [3]
Reviewer corrections Missed or extra boxes Sampled 0.1-1% of output Gold set for monitoring assumption
Synthetic Pasted faces and plates, rendered weather Unlimited Fills rare slices assumption
Active learning Uncertain-band boxes sent to annotators Ongoing Cuts labelling cost; human-in-the-loop loop in ByteByteGo's refs [6]

Features

Feature Type Used by Notes
RGB pixels (tile) Tensor Backbone Main signal, multi-scale
Image pyramid level / tile coords Integer Merge step Maps boxes back to the panorama
Camera id, lens, projection Categorical Preprocess Corrects equirectangular distortion
GPS / country Categorical Thresholds, plate model Per-region plate formats
Time of day, weather Categorical Eval slices Night recall drops
Neighbour-frame boxes Boxes Temporal consistency The same face seen from the next capture point

Model choices (baseline -> advanced)

Stage Model Pros Cons Source
Baseline Haar / HOG sliding window + classifier (Viola-Jones style) Cheap, explainable Low recall on profile and small faces [2]
Two-stage Faster R-CNN + FPN High accuracy, good on small objects. ByteByteGo's pick for offline batch Slower, two-step training [1] [14] [16]
Cascade Cascade R-CNN Better localisation at high IoU More compute [19]
One-stage RetinaNet / YOLO / SSD Fast, simple. Focal loss handles class imbalance Historically weaker on tiny objects [15] [17]
Specialist RetinaFace for faces + plate detector Best per-class recall Two models to run [20]
Transformer DETR / ViTDet No anchors or NMS (DETR); strong scaling Slow convergence, compute-heavy [21] [22]
Ensemble Union of detectors -> verifier Maximises recall Cost, more false positives assumption
Open-source reference Meta EgoBlur face + plate detectors Pretrained, released for privacy use Tuned to egocentric Aria imagery [25]

Loss

Component Loss Why
Classification Cross-entropy over {bg, face, plate}, or focal loss Background dominates, and focal loss down-weights easy negatives [15]
Box regression Smooth L1 on (dx, dy, dw, dh), or GIoU / CIoU GIoU is aligned with the IoU metric [23]
RPN (two-stage) BCE objectness + smooth L1 Proposal quality
Recall bias Class weights / lower positive IoU threshold for faces A missed face costs more than an extra blur

Offline metrics

Metric Definition Target / use
IoU Area of overlap / area of union Match threshold, usually 0.5 [1]
Precision, recall At IoU >= 0.5 Report recall at a fixed precision (for example 0.98 recall at P >= 0.8)
AP / mAP Area under the PR curve, averaged over classes (and IoU 0.5:0.95 COCO-style) Main model-selection metric [1]
Recall by object size Small (<16 px), medium, large Tiny far faces are the hardest slice
COCO-style AP AP@[0.5:0.95], AP_small/medium/large Standard detection eval protocol [6]
Slice recall Country, skin tone, night, occlusion, plate format Fairness and coverage gates
Pixel coverage Fraction of face pixels covered by any blur Partial blur still counts as a leak

Online metrics / A-B

Metric Definition Notes
User privacy reports per 1M images "Report a problem" blur requests Main online signal [1] [3]
Reviewer-measured miss rate Missed faces or plates in an audited sample Gold metric, not delayed
Over-blur rate Blurred non-targets (signs, posters) Hurts imagery usefulness
Throughput / cost Images per GPU-hour, backlog age Publication SLA
A-B method Not user-randomised. Use a shadow run on a holdout region plus a human audit of disagreements between old and new models No traffic split needed

Serving & latency budget (per panorama, batch)

Step Budget Hardware / note
Fetch + decode + reproject 0.3-0.5 s CPU workers
Tiling + pyramid (about 40-80 tiles) 0.1 s CPU
Detection (batched tiles) 0.5-2 s GPU/TPU, FP16/INT8, batch 16-64
Merge + NMS + policy <0.1 s CPU
Blur render + write 0.2 s CPU
End-to-end About 1-3 s compute; wall-clock SLA hours Throughput matters, latency does not
Scale check 1M panos/day x 2 s = about 23 GPU-days/day, so about 25-50 GPUs assumption

Monitoring

Signal Alert on
Boxes per panorama (by class, region) Sudden drop means a model or camera regression
Score distribution Shift (new camera hardware, new country)
Reviewer miss rate on the gold sample Above the SLA, for example >1% missed faces
User report rate Spike by region or capture batch
Pipeline health Backlog age, failed shards, GPU utilisation
Data drift New plate formats, snow or night share, new lens

Failure modes

Failure Cause Mitigation
Missed tiny or distant faces Low resolution High-res tiles, P2 FPN level, multi-scale test-time augmentation
Faces split across tile seams Tiling Overlap tiles, merge with NMS in panorama coordinates
Equirectangular distortion at poles Projection Cube-map reprojection
False positives on posters, statues, billboards Face-like patterns Hard-negative mining. Over-blur is acceptable, so bias toward blurring
Blurring signs or business names Plate-like text Verifier, context features
Foreign plate formats Domain shift Per-country data, region thresholds
Demographic recall gaps Biased training data Stratified labelling, slice gates
Partial blur leaks identity Tight box Expand box margin, pixel-coverage metric
De-blurring attack Weak blur Irreversible blur (pixelate + noise), never ship the raw image
Model upgrade un-blurs Replace instead of union Union old and new boxes; boxes only ever get added

Interviewer follow-ups

  • Why prioritise recall over precision, and how do you pick the operating threshold?
  • Two-stage vs one-stage detector for an offline batch job: which and why? [1]
  • How does NMS work, what goes wrong with crowds, and when would you use soft-NMS? [24]
  • How do you handle 100-megapixel panoramas: downscale, tile, or multi-scale?
  • How do you avoid duplicate or split boxes at tile boundaries?
  • How do you get 1M labelled images cheaply? Active learning, pseudo-labels, user reports.
  • How do you split train and test to avoid leakage between neighbouring frames of one street?
  • mAP vs recall-at-precision: which do you report to the privacy team?
  • How do you measure and guarantee recall across skin tones and countries?
  • How would you A-B test a new model when there is no click signal?
  • How do you backfill tens of billions of images when the model improves, and at what cost?
  • How do you handle user requests to blur a whole house or car (out of model scope)?
  • How would you run this on the capture vehicle (edge) instead of in the data centre?
  • How would you extend it to new classes (house numbers, screens, ID cards)?
  • How do GDPR and "right to be forgotten" requests change raw-data retention and training-set reuse? [6]
  • How do you train on about 1M high-res images: data parallel vs model parallel? [6]
  • Which samples go to annotators first (active learning on the uncertain band)? [6]
  • How do you detect drift when new camera hardware ships?

Portal comparison

Portal Framing Model Metrics Distinctive points
ByteByteGo ch. 4 [1] Batch privacy pipeline, 2 classes, about 1M labelled images Two-stage (Faster R-CNN-like), compared with one-stage IoU, precision, AP, mAP offline; user reports online Full walk-through of NMS, augmentation, hard negatives, batch vs online prediction
Google ICCV 2009 (real system) [2] Production privacy at Street View scale Sliding-window detectors + post-processing classifier; separate plate detector Recall of about 89% faces, 94-96% plates Shows that recall-first operating points plus a manual-report path are the norm
Educative Grokking [7] Self-driving perception (segmentation / detection) CNN encoder-decoder, detectors IoU, pixel accuracy Same CV building blocks, real-time edge setting
alirezadir MLSD [4] Generic template plus a CV detection cheat sheet R-CNN family, YOLO, SSD mAP, IoU Concise checklists, no full case
Exponent / Hello Interview [8] [9] Delivery framework applied to any prompt Model-agnostic Business vs model metrics Interview pacing and communication
Meta EgoBlur (real system) [25] Privacy blurring for egocentric AR data Separate face and plate detectors Not stated on repo page Open-source weights; shows the same 2-class design in production

18. Design Search Query Autocomplete / Typeahead with ML Ranking

Source note: refs [1] [3] [5] [6] [14] [15] were fetched for this review. Several other domains (arXiv, ByteByteGo, Google, LinkedIn, Instacart, Algolia) could not be reached from this run; those references are well-known primary sources, and the Instacart and Algolia URLs are confirmed by the index in [15]. Rows marked "(assumption)" are typical interview defaults, not cited figures.

Company tags

Company / context What links it to this problem Source
Google (Search, Gmail) Chip Huyen's exercise #5 uses Google's related searches. Gmail Smart Compose is the production neural-completion reference [3] [9] [10]
Amazon (product search) Session-aware QAC built as extreme multi-label ranking (KDD 2021) [7]
Microsoft (Bing) Personalized QAC learning-to-rank (SIGIR 2013) and rare-prefix QAC (CIKM 2015) [5] [6]
LinkedIn Partial, out-of-order, real-time typeahead over connections, companies, groups, skills (Cleo, open-sourced 2012) [8] [14]
Instacart ML-driven autocomplete for grocery search (2022) [11]
Algolia (SaaS search) Query Suggestions product built from search analytics [12]
Meta, Uber, DoorDash, etc. Often reported on forums as a search sub-problem. Not verified for this chapter (unverified)

Portals that cover it

  • alirezadir / AIMLInterviews lists "Autocompletion / typeahead suggestion system" as an NLP sample MLSD question [1].
  • Chip Huyen, ML Systems Design exercises #5 (related searches) and #10 ("finish your sentence when you text") [3] [4].
  • ByteByteGo / Alex Xu, System Design Interview Vol. 1, Ch. 13 "Design a Search Autocomplete System". This is the trie/infra version that most ML answers build on [2].
  • DesignGurus / Educative Grokking, "Designing Typeahead Suggestion" (infra version) [13].
  • Engineer1999 curated case-study list (Instacart, Algolia entries) [15].

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Source
Functional Return the top-K (5-10) completions for a prefix on every keystroke. Personalized, fresh (trending), safe [2] [5]
Optional Spelling-tolerant prefixes, entity suggestions (people, products), multi-language [8] (assumption)
ML objective Rank candidate completions by P(user selects completion and the search succeeds) [5] [7]
DAU 10M users, 10 searches/day, about 20 chars/query, one request per keystroke [2]
QPS About 24k QPS average and about 48k peak in the Xu estimate. FAANG-scale is more than 100k (assumption) [2]
Latency Under 100 ms end-to-end, or the suggestions feel laggy. Model budget 5-20 ms (assumption) [2]
Candidate pool 10M-1B distinct historical queries. Top-N per prefix is precomputed [2] (assumption)
Freshness Trending queries surface within minutes. Base index rebuilt daily or weekly [2] (assumption)
Non-functional Highly available, safe (no offensive or defamatory completions), privacy (no PII leakage) (assumption)

What production systems add beyond the portal answers

System Addition often missed in interviews Source
Bing (Shokouhi 2013) Supervised personal ranker with a labeling strategy for offline data. Long-term history and location matter most. Up to 9% MRR gain over popularity [5]
Bing (Mitra & Craswell 2015) Synthetic candidates from mined query suffixes for unseen prefixes, ranked with n-gram and CLSM features [6]
Amazon (Yadav et al. 2021) Previous query in the session as input to an XMR model that retrieves completions directly [7]
LinkedIn Cleo Partial and out-of-order token matching, real-time index updates, one library across many entity types [8] [14]
Gmail Smart Compose Neural LM completion under a strict per-keystroke latency budget, with safety filtering of generated text [9] [10]

Data & labels

Item Choice Note
Unit of example (prefix, candidate, user, context) at each keystroke impression [5]
Positive Shown completion the user selected Selection is the direct signal
Weak positive Final submitted query that starts with the prefix but was not shown Recovers recall when the user kept typing [5]
Negative Shown, not selected Position bias: down-weight or use IPS
Label weight Boost when the downstream search succeeded (click, purchase) [11] (assumption)
Cold data Synthetic prefixes from full queries (all prefixes of q) Standard bootstrap
Public benchmark AOL query log (used with Bing logs in Shokouhi 2013) [5]

Features

Group Examples
Popularity Global and per-geo frequency, time-decayed count, hourly trend velocity
Prefix-query Completion length, prefix ends mid-word, fuzzy-match distance, out-of-order token match [14]
Suffix / semantic N-gram suffix frequency, CLSM similarity of prefix and candidate (rare prefixes) [6]
Personal Past issuance of q by user, recency, long-term history and location (the strongest personal signals in [5])
Session Sim to previous queries in session, reformulation patterns [7]
Quality Historical CTR at position, zero-result rate, downstream conversion [11]
Context Time of day, device, locale, surface (web, app, voice)

Model choices

Stage Option Pros Cons
Baseline MostPopularCompletion from a trie Simple, under 1 ms Not personal, fails on rare prefixes
Retrieval Trie/FST with precomputed top-N per node [2] O(prefix len) lookup Fixed vocab, rebuild cost
Retrieval Suffix synthesis for rare prefixes [6] Covers the long tail Can produce nonsense
Retrieval XMR / extreme classification [7] Uses session context Training complexity
Ranker GBDT LambdaMART Strong on tabular features, cheap Weak on raw text
Ranker Two-tower / cross DNN Semantic and session aware Latency, needs GPU or quantization
Generator Char/subword LM + beam [9][10] Open vocabulary Safety risk, ms per token

Loss

Model Loss
LTR ranker Pairwise (RankNet) or LambdaRank/LambdaMART optimizing nDCG / MRR
Pointwise alt Binary cross-entropy on selected vs shown, IPS-weighted
Generator Token-level cross-entropy (next-char / next-token)
Safety filter Binary or multi-label cross-entropy

Offline metrics

Metric Meaning
MRR Reciprocal rank of the eventually-submitted query [5]
Success@K / Recall@K Target query appears in the top K
pSaved / eSaved Probability-weighted keystrokes saved
nDCG@K Graded by downstream success
Safety rate Percent of prefixes that produce an offensive completion (red-team set)
Coverage Percent of prefixes with at least 1 suggestion (rare-prefix tail) [6]

Online metrics / A/B

Metric Type
Suggestion CTR / acceptance rate Primary
Keystrokes per search, time to search Primary (effort)
Downstream search success (click, purchase), reformulation rate North star
Zero-result searches Guardrail
p99 latency, error rate Guardrail
Offensive-suggestion reports Safety guardrail

Serving & latency budget

Step Budget (assumption)
Client debounce + network 30-50 ms
Edge/prefix cache lookup 1-2 ms (high hit rate for short prefixes)
Candidate gen (trie + trending + personal, parallel) 5-10 ms
Filtering 1-2 ms
Feature fetch 3-5 ms
Ranker on ~200 candidates 5-15 ms (GBDT or a distilled DNN)
Re-rank / policy 1 ms
Total server Under 40 ms. End-to-end under 100 ms [2]

Monitoring

What Signal
Data Log volume per keystroke, label join rate, feature null rate
Model Score distribution drift, MRR on fresh holdout, CTR by position
Freshness Lag from trending event to suggestion
Safety Blocklist hits, user reports, sensitive-entity completions
System Cache hit rate, p50/p99 latency, shard hotness

Failure modes

Failure Mitigation
Offensive, defamatory or PII completions Blocklists, classifier, human escalation, takedown pipeline
Rich-get-richer / position-bias loop IPS, randomized exploration slots, counterfactual LTR
Rare or new prefixes return nothing Suffix synthesis [6], neural generator, fuzzy match
Trending spikes missed Streaming counts with time decay
Manipulation (query spam to push a completion) Unique-user thresholds, anomaly detection
Latency spikes on 1-char prefixes Precompute and cache short prefixes at the edge
Personal leakage on shared devices Per-account history, opt-out, no cross-user PII

Interviewer follow-ups

  • How do you generate labels when the user never clicks a suggestion and keeps typing?
  • How do you correct for position bias in the selection logs?
  • How do you handle a prefix never seen before (long tail)? [6]
  • Trie with precomputed top-N vs on-the-fly ranking: what goes where? [2]
  • How do you surface a breaking-news query within 5 minutes?
  • How would you personalize without hurting the cache hit rate? [5]
  • How do you use the previous query in the session? [7]
  • How do you prevent offensive or legally risky completions?
  • Would you use an LLM to generate completions? What are the latency and safety costs? [9]
  • What offline metric best predicts online keystrokes saved?
  • How do you handle typos in the prefix ("iphnoe")?
  • How do you match out-of-order tokens ("york new" to "new york")? [14]
  • Personalized ranker vs popularity: what gain is realistic? (Up to 9% MRR on Bing logs) [5]
  • How do you support multiple languages and scripts (CJK input methods)?
  • How do you stop adversaries from gaming the suggestions?
  • How do you shard the index and keep it consistent during rebuilds?

DesignGurus / Grokking [13] Infra system design Trie, offline aggregation, partitioning, client-side tricks Popularity only

19. Design Music Recommendation and Playlist Generation (Spotify Discover Weekly and Home)

How the prompt is usually worded: "Design Spotify's 'Discover Weekly' playlist" [1][2], or "Design the Spotify Home page: which shelves and which playlists or tracks each user sees". Variants: automatic playlist continuation ("add songs to this playlist") [22][23], radio or autoplay (next-track), "Daily Mix", podcast recommendations on Home [11][12], and conversational music recommendation (Amazon Music) [26].

Sourcing note: this chapter was compiled and reviewed after the shared web-search budget had run out. Only GitHub hosts could be reached. engineering.atspotify.com, dl.acm.org, hackernoon.com and amazon.science did not resolve when re-checked in review. Sources marked (fetched) were read for this chapter through GitHub. Sources marked (ch-ref) were verified in earlier chapters of this atlas. Sources marked (known) are canonical papers or posts whose URLs were confirmed through curated GitHub lists [24][25] but whose text could not be re-read here. Numbers taken from them are flagged.

Company tags

Company What is reported Source
Spotify The problem is Spotify's own product. "Design Spotify's 'Discover Weekly' playlist" appears in community MLSD question lists as a standard recommendation prompt [1][2][3]
Meta A company-tagged question bank lists "Design Spotify" (system design, medium) under Meta. This is the classic (non-ML) version; an open-source "Design Spotify" answer adds a GET /api/recommendations/discover-weekly endpoint, so the recommender is a natural deep-dive [4][35]
Amazon (Amazon Music), Apple (Apple Music), YouTube Music, Pandora, Deezer, SoundCloud These companies run the same kind of product. No direct question report could be verified for this chapter, so treat this row as an inference assumption
General MLE loops One community guide asserts that almost every MLSD round includes a prompt such as "Design Spotify's Discover Weekly" (opinion, no data) [2]

Portals and sources that cover it

Portal / source Treatment Link
Community MLSD notes (sharayu134, mdrijwan123, Gaurav14cs17) [1] lists "Design Spotify's 'Discover Weekly' playlist" as a sample prompt; [2] cites Discover Weekly as a recsys impact example; [3] lists "Spotify: Discover Weekly hybrid approach" as a case study [1][2][3]
Chip Huyen (DMLS book resources) Lists the Ciocca Discover Weekly article (CF + NLP + audio models) as reading. Her MLSD booklet [34] is generic and has no music content [5][6]
ByteByteGo (Aminian & Xu) No music chapter. Use the video-recommendation chapter (two-tower retrieval plus ranker) as the template [28]
alirezadir AIMLInterviews Video and game recommendation templates. No music file [27]
Hello Interview Generic recommendation-systems pattern (retrieval, ranking, re-ranking); no music write-up. See also E. Yan on discovery system design [30][32]
Exponent / Aced, Educative Generic MLSD frameworks. No music-specific write-up could be verified [29][31]
Spotify engineering and research (the real system) Discover Weekly hybrid (CF + NLP + audio), BaRT bandits on Home, CoSeRNN contextual user embeddings, Annoy then Voyager ANN, in-house experimentation platform [6]-[20], [36]

Requirements & scale

Dimension Value Basis
Functional (a) Discover Weekly: 30 new-to-user tracks per user, refreshed every Monday. (b) Home: rank shelves (cards) and the items inside each shelf. (c) Explain the slot ("Because you listened to X") [6][8] (known)
Novelty constraint Discover Weekly must exclude tracks the user has already played. Home can mix familiar and new content [6] (known)
Users Hundreds of millions of MAU. Assume 600M+ users and 100M+ tracks, plus podcasts and audiobooks typical assumption
Weekly batch 600M users x 30 tracks = about 18B rows of slate per week. Spread over a 2-3 day batch window assumption
Home QPS About 50k QPS peak for Home loads, with 10-20 shelves per page assumption
Latency Home p99 under 200 ms server-side. Discover Weekly is offline (precomputed), with a single key-value read at request time assumption
ANN scale Spotify's Voyager is "queried hundreds of millions of times per day" [19] (fetched)
Historical reach Discover Weekly "reaches over 30 million users every week" (older figure quoted by a community guide) [2] (fetched)
Non-functional Freshness (new releases, new users), diversity and artist fairness, explainability, cost of weekly batch, privacy [8][16] (known)
